sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Activation of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/AKT (PI3K/AKT) signaling pathway promotes tumor immune evasion by suppressing effector T-cell infiltration and enhancing regulatory T-cell (Treg) activity, contributing to resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that inhibition of this pathway can restore antitumor immunity and synergize with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. We explore the synergistic clinical potential of targeting the PI3K/AKT pathway in combination with atezolizumab to overcome immunotherapy resistance in recurrent glioblastoma (GBM) and advanced solid tumors.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: Phase Ib, investigator-initiated, open-label study (NCT03673787) composed of a proof-of-concept dose escalation part A of ipatasertib plus atezolizumab in a 3 + 3 design. Adult patients with treatment-refractory advanced cancers were enrolled into cohort A1 and recurrent GBM into cohort A2. Part B enrolled patients into six exploratory cohorts. The study aims to evaluate the safety, immune-modulatory effects, and preliminary efficacy of the combination of ipatasertib with atezolizumab.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: The combination was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities at the recommended phase II dose of ipatasertib 400 mg daily plus atezolizumab 1,200 mg every 3 weeks. Pharmacodynamic analysis demonstrated depletion of FOXP3+ Tregs and increased infiltration of CD8+ effector T cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Durable exceptional responses were seen in some patients with treatment-refractory or recurrent GBM.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: This is the first report in clinical samples showing that ipatasertib efficiently depletes FOXP3+ Tregs and results in increased infiltration of effector CD8+ T cells in the TME. This was associated with preliminary efficacy in a subset of patients with treatment-refractory GBM.

boxed-text.p: This study provides preliminary clinical evidence that blockade of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway can remodel the immunosuppressive TME and potentially overcome resistance to ICIs in malignant recurrent GBM. The combination of the selective AKT inhibitor ipatasertib with the anti–PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab was well tolerated and demonstrated robust immunomodulatory activity, including depletion of FOXP3+ Tregs and increased infiltration of effector CD8+ T cells within the TME, independent of PI3K mutational status or phosphatase and tensin homolog loss. Durable and exceptional clinical responses were observed in a subset of patients with recurrent, treatment-refractory disease. These results highlight PI3K/AKT pathway inhibition as a mechanistically rational and clinically feasible strategy warranting broader evaluation in this cancer of unmet need.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT signaling pathway regulates a wide range of cellular processes, including growth and survival (1, 2). Hyperactivation of this pathway is a critical driver of tumorigenesis, with phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) being one of the most common targets of mutation/deletion in human tumors. Other mechanisms of PI3K/AKT pathway deregulation include PIK3CA mutations, AKT amplification and mutations, and overexpression (transcriptional upregulation) and activation downstream of the AKT pathway (3). Deregulation of this pathway is a frequent hallmark of tumor resistance to chemotherapy, targeted therapies, and, more recently, immunotherapy (4–6).

The PI3K/AKT pathway has been implicated in the regulation of both innate and adaptive immunity and plays crucial roles in immune cell maturation, differentiation, recruitment, and survival (5). AKT has also been shown to control regulatory T cell (Treg) homeostasis through inhibitory phosphorylation of FOXO1, which, in turn, promotes immune tolerance by restraining immune effector cells (7–11).

Despite the successes of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 checkpoints, many cancers do not respond or respond incompletely to immunotherapy (12, 13). Although a myriad of mechanisms can underlie ICI treatment failure, the profound immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) rich in inhibitory Tregs has been associated with hyperactive PI3K/AKT signaling. Thus, ICI resistance may be reversible by blockade of this pathway (14–18). Preclinical studies in multiple solid tumor models have shown increasing evidence that targeting the PI3K/AKT pathway, and AKT in particular, can reduce the production of immunosuppressive cytokines such as IL10 and TGFβ (19–21). Reduction of IL10 and TGFβ restricts the proliferation and penetration of immunosuppressive Tregs and inhibits M2 macrophage polarization, boosting the antitumor effects of immune checkpoint blockade (22, 23). Coinhibition of the PI3K pathway has improved the efficacy of anti–PD-1 and anti–CTLA-4 antibodies in PTEN-driven murine models of melanoma (24), as well as in syngeneic murine models of breast and lung cancer (25, 26). Additionally, the pharmacologic inhibition of the PI3K/AKT pathway in in vitro patient cell assays showed inhibition and reduction in Treg populations and enhancement of the CD8+ memory T-derived tissue (27). Given that many of the immunosuppressive effects of PI3K activation seem to be mediated by AKT and because AKT inhibitors seem to be generally safer compared with PI3K inhibitors, combination strategies using AKT inhibitors are likely preferable (28).

We conducted an open-label proof-of-concept phase Ib clinical trial to interrogate the effect of PI3K/AKT blockade on the immune system and its synergy with ICIs for effective cancer immunotherapy. Mandatory serial blood and tumor sampling allowed for comprehensive translational analyses.

We report, for the first time, the safety and tolerability of the combination of ipatasertib, a potent AKT inhibitor, with the anti–PD-L1 ICI, atezolizumab, and describe the pharmacodynamic effects of PI3K/AKT blockade on the immune system and the TME. We report preliminary efficacy in a subset of patients with treatment-refractory glioblastoma (GBM).

sec.title: Patients and Methods
sec.p: The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles derived from international guidelines, including the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Medicines and Health products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and the ethics committee, and all patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This was an open-label, single-center phase I study in patients with treatment-refractory advanced solid tumors and GBM (ICE-CAP, Ipatasertib in Combination with Atezolizumab in PI3K pathway hyperactivated tumors; NCT03673787). The trial commenced in August 2018 and contained two parts: (i) Part A: proof-of-concept dose exploration of the combination of oral ipatasertib given continuously with three weekly doses of atezolizumab 1,200 mg intravenously. Dose escalation decisions for the patients with solid tumors in cohort A1 were guided by a 3 + 3 design, whereas patients with GBM in cohort A2 were enrolled at the dose level cleared in cohort A1. (ii) Part B enrolled patients into six exploratory cohorts (Fig. 1A). Data presented here are from part A and the GBM exploratory cohort B3 as of September 2024.

sec.p: The primary objectives of the dose exploration part were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of the combination of ipatasertib and atezolizumab and to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and the recommended phase II dose (RP2D). The secondary objectives were to characterize the pharmacodynamic effects of PI3K/AKT blockade by single-agent ipatasertib and the combination with atezolizumab on immune parameters in blood and tumor. Tertiary objectives were to obtain a preliminary assessment of antitumor efficacy in patients with tumors resistant to ICIs.

sec.title: Patient selection
sec.p: Adult patients aged ≥18 years were included if they had histologically or cytologically confirmed advanced solid cancer refractory to standard therapy. Patients enrolled in cohort A1 needed to have biopsiable disease, whereas patients with GBM enrolled in part A2 needed to have disease potentially suitable for re-resection/surgical biopsy. Key inclusion criteria also required that patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group functional status of 0 or 1 and had adequate organ function. Key exclusion criteria were autoimmune disorders requiring immunosuppression. Full eligibility criteria are further detailed in the Supplementary Methods.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: Ipatasertib was administered orally daily in 21-day cycles, and atezolizumab was administered as an intravenous infusion every 21 days. Dose escalation commenced at the minimum anticipated biological effect level—defined as the starting dose of ipatasertib (200 mg daily continuously)—and progressed according to the dosing schema to 400 mg daily continuously.
Patients in part A were given a run-in period with ipatasertib monotherapy of 14 to 21 days (Fig. 1A) to allow for the collection of serial blood and tumor samples for pharmacodynamic analyses.

sec.title: Analysis populations
sec.p: All safety endpoints were summarized using the safety population, which comprised all patients who had received at least one dose of ipatasertib or one dose of atezolizumab and who had at least one postdosing safety evaluation.

All baseline characteristics and demographics are reported per the safety evaluable population; efficacy data are reported as per the efficacy evaluable population; and pharmacodynamic data were analyzed using the tissue available population (Supplementary Tables S1 and S2). For part A, all patients who had completed the cycle 1 dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) period (i.e., 35 days) and received at least 75% of the specified dose of ipatasertib (i.e., at least 27 doses out of the planned 35) and received the cycle 1 day 1 dose of atezolizumab were considered evaluable for the purposes of dose escalation decisions. For part B dose expansion, the population comprised all patients who received at least one partial or complete cycle of ipatasertib and atezolizumab combination therapy.

sec.title: Efficacy analysis
sec.p: Efficacy analysis included the assessment of objective response (OR), duration of response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) from the start of combination treatment. OR was assessed as per immune-modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors criteria or immunotherapy Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (iRANO) criteria (29, 30). Radiographic tumor burden assessments were conducted by the investigator and could include CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and bone scans. Assessments were performed at baseline, at week 9 and every subsequent 9 weeks until study discontinuation. Details of imaging acquisition are provided in the supplementary data.

sec.title: Statistical considerations
sec.p: The sample size in the dose-exploration proof-of-concept part A was based on practical considerations and was consistent with conventional oncology studies with the objective of estimating the MTD and obtaining proof of mechanism. Two dose levels were explored, starting at the minimum biologically active dose and escalated per the 3 + 3 design following review by the Safety Review Committee.

sec.title: Peripheral blood lymphocyte profiling
sec.p: In part A, to assess the effect of single-agent AKT inhibition, whole peripheral blood was collected at baseline (cycle 1 day 14 for cohort A1 or cycle 1 day 21 for cohort A2) and after 14 to 21 days of continuous ipatasertib monotherapy (before infusion on cycle 1 day 1 or 48 hours prior to surgery for cohort A2). Subsequent samples to assess the effect of the combination of AKT inhibition and atezolizumab were collected on day 1 of each cycle until treatment discontinuation. Samples were stained with monoclonal antibodies against the following cell surface markers: CD3, CD4, CD8, CD5, CD56, CD19, CD20, and CD45. Stained cells were acquired and analyzed on a CytoFLEX LX (Beckman Coulter) cytometer using Kaluza version 2.1 software (RRID:SCR_016182).

sec.title: Serum cytokine profiling
sec.p: Blood samples for cytokine profiling were collected in 5 mL BD SST II Plus Vacutainer tubes at the same time points listed above. Cytokine concentrations (pg/mL) were measured by the multiplex MesoScale Discovery V-Plex Plus Human Pro-Inflammatory Panel 1 Kit (K15049G), customized by MSD to detect only for IFNγ, IL1β, IL2, IL6, IL8, IL10, and TNFα. Log2 fold changes of cytokine concentrations from baseline (cycle 1 day 14 or cycle 1 day 21) to post-ipatasertib (cycle 1 day 1) were calculated for each patient. Concentrations below the lower limit of quantification were included in the calculations. Concentrations below the assay lower limit of detection (LLOD) were set as the LLOD value. Patients 101-051 and 101-057 were excluded as post-ipatasertib samples were not available. TNFα concentrations for patient 101-038 were excluded due to quality control failure. Comparisons were performed using a paired t test, with a P value of 0.05 being statistically significant.

sec.title: Tumor analysis
sec.p: Mandatory paired tumor biopsies were collected from all patients enrolled in cohort A1 at baseline and following 14 days of continuous ipatasertib monotherapy, with additional optional biopsies collected after the first cycle of combination ipatasertib and atezolizumab. At each time point, two needle core biopsies (size 14–16 gauge) were taken under ultrasound guidance. Three 3 μm sections of tumor were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), and the presence of tumor was confirmed by a pathologist (B. Gurel). Paired samples were analyzed by multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) for tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL). A formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) block was submitted to HistoGeneX for immunophenotyping, PD-L1 assessment, and nucleic acid extraction. RNA and whole-exome sequencing were performed by Q Squared Solutions. Patients with GBM in cohorts A2 and B3 provided archival FFPE samples for similar analyses, as well as IHC for PTEN status. Patients with potentially resectable disease who had agreed to proceed to surgery had tumor cores collected for analyses.

sec.title: 5-Plex IF (CD3, CD4, CD8, FOXP3, and pan-cytokeratin) for cohort A1
sec.p: TILs were determined by mIF for T-cell subpopulations as previously described (31). mIF staining was performed on 3 μm FFPE tissue sections using an automated staining platform (BOND RX, Leica Microsystems). Antigen retrieval was achieved using BOND Epitope Retrieval Solution 2 (#AR9640, Leica Biosystems). Endogenous peroxidase was inactivated in 3% H2O2. Tissue sections were incubated with antibodies against CD4 (#ab133616, clone EPR6855, Abcam) and CD8 (#M7103, clone C8/144B, Dako, Agilent Technologies; RRID:SCR_013575) and detected with Alexa Fluor 555–conjugated IgG (H + L) goat anti-rabbit (#A21429, Invitrogen; RRID:AB_2535850) and Alexa Fluor 488–conjugated IgG (H + L) goat anti-mouse (#A-11029, Invitrogen; RRID:AB_2534088) secondary antibodies, respectively. Endogenous biotin was blocked with an avidin/biotin blocking kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol (#ab64212, Abcam). Tissue sections were incubated with antibodies against FOXP3 conjugated to biotin (#13-4777-82, clone 236A/E7, eBioscience, Thermo Fisher Scientific; RRID:AB_466655) and pan-cytokeratin (PanCK) conjugated to Alexa Fluor 647 (#4528S, clone C11, Cell Signaling Technology; RRID:AB_836890), followed by streptavidin peroxidase (horseradish peroxidase; #K5001, Dako, Agilent Technologies) and the TSA Coumarin detection system (#NEL703001KT, Akoya Biosciences). Nuclei were counterstained with DRAQ 7 (#DR71000, Biostatus), and tissue sections were mounted with ProLong Gold antifade reagent (#P36930, Molecular Probes).

Slides were scanned using the Vectra Automated Multispectral Imaging System (Akoya Biosciences) and analyzed using inForm version 2.2.1 (Akoya Biosciences). Tissue and nuclear cell segmentation were performed using previously described methods (32). TIL phenotype determination was based on staining for CD8, CD4, and FOXP3 and was separated into bins as follows: CD8+, CD4+FOXP3+, and CD4+FOXP3− T cells.

sec.title: 4-Plex IF (CD3, CD4, CD8, and FOXP3) for cohorts A2 and B3
sec.p: 4-Plex OPAL-based sequential IF staining was performed on the Bond RX automated staining platform (Leica Biosystems). Three 3 μm FFPE tissue sections underwent heat-induced epitope retrieval with BOND epitope retrieval solution 2 (pH 9.0; #AR9640, Leica Biosystems) for 20 minutes), followed by endogenous peroxidase blocking (Novocastra Peroxidase Block, #RE7157, Leica Biosystems) for 10 minutes. Nonspecific antibody binding was blocked using Opal Antibody Diluent/Block (ARD1001EA, Akoya Biosciences) for 10 minutes. Primary antibodies against CD3 (#A0452, Rabbit Polyclonal Antibody, Dako, RRID:AB_2335677), CD4 (#ab133616, clone EPR6855, Abcam, RRID:AB_2750883), CD8 (#M7103, clone C8/144B, Dako, Agilent Technologies, RRID:AB_2075537), and FOXP3 (#14-4777-82, clone 236A/E7, eBioscience, Thermo Fisher Scientific, RRID:AB_467556) were sequentially incubated for 30 minutes, followed by detection with the Novolink Max Polymer Detection System (RE7280-K, Leica Biosystems). mIF signals for CD8, CD4, FOXP3, and CD3 were visualized using OPAL 520, OPAL 570, OPAL 620, and OPAL 690 (NEL871001KT, Opal 6-Plex Detection Kit, Akoya Biosciences), respectively, and counterstained with spectral DAPI (FP1490, Akoya Biosciences). Automated imaging was performed on the PhenoCycler-Fusion system (Akoya Biosciences) using the instrument controller software version 1.0.7 (Akoya Biosciences).

mIF images were reviewed by a pathologist (B. Gurel). Analysis was performed using HALO image analysis software (Indica Labs). Cell detection was based on nuclear DAPI counterstain, with nuclear diameter thresholds of 8 μm (minimum) and 25 μm (maximum). Nuclear segmentation parameters were optimized to detect individual nuclei while minimizing oversegmentation of clustered cells. Cell phenotyping used intensity thresholds for each fluorescence channel (OPAL 520, 570, 620, and 690), which were set by comparing signal intensities in positive and negative control tissue sections stained on the same slides. These thresholds remained constant across all analyzed images. T lymphocyte populations were classified using Boolean logic based on marker combinations: CD3+CD4+CD8−FOXP3− (Th cells), CD3+CD4−CD8+FOXP3− (cytotoxic T cells), and CD3+CD4+FOXP3+ (Tregs). The accuracy of cell classification was verified through manual review of representative image fields.

sec.title: 4-Plex IF (macrophages) for cohorts A2 and B3
sec.p: 4-Plex OPAL-based sequential IF staining was carried out on the Bond RX automated staining platform (Leica Biosystems). FFPE tissue sections of 3 μm underwent heat-induced epitope retrieval with epitope retrieval solution 1 (pH 6.0; No. AR9961, ER1, Leica Biosystems) followed by endogenous peroxidase blocking (Novocastra Peroxidase Block, No. RE7157, Leica Biosystems) for 10 minutes. Nonspecific antibody binding was blocked using OPAL antibody diluent/block (ARD1001EA, Akoya Biosciences) for 10 minutes. Primary antibodies against CD206/MRC1 (Cell Signaling Technology, #91992, 1:250; RRID:AB_2800175), CD68 (Dako #M0876, 1:200; RRID:AB_2074844), and CD163 (Abcam, #ab182422, 1:200; RRID:AB_2753196) were sequentially incubated for 30 minutes, followed by detection with the Novolink Max Polymer Detection System (RE7280-K, Leica Biosystems). IF signals for CD206, CD68, and CD163 were visualized using OPAL 520 (NEL820001KT, Akoya Biosciences), OPAL 570 (NEL820001KT, Akoya Biosciences), and OPAL 650 (FP1496001KT, Akoya Biosciences), respectively, and counterstained with spectral DAPI. Slides were scanned using the VS200 Research Slide Scanner (Olympus).
Exploratory statistical analysis of immune cell counts from multiplex IF and flow cytometry was performed using a two-tailed unpaired t test with GraphPad Prism (RRID:SCR_002798).

sec.title: PD-L1 and immune phenotyping
sec.p: FFPE samples were submitted to HistoGeneX for analysis according to their standard operating procedures. This included H&E assessment, PD-L1 SP263 IHC, and PanCK/CD8 IHC. Cytoplasmic staining was not included in the scoring (TE-IQ-16 method on FO-390, HistoGeneX). The PanCK-CD8 IHC slides were evaluated for CD8 using the universal immune cell marker scoring algorithm (TE-IQ-40 and FO-526, HistoGeneX). The output of this analysis was the relative surface area (%) of the tumor with a CD8+ immune cell density that belongs to one of the eight density bins and for each of the eight density bins (eight data fields per IHC slide). The density bins were linked to marker-specific (CD8) reference images that were used by the pathologist. The immune phenotype was scored as “desert,” “inflamed,” or “excluded” (two types: invasive margin and intratumoral). PanCK was automatically detected to generate an epithelial carcinoma mask in the annotated tumor region. The relative surface area of CD8+ TILs was then measured in both stromal and epithelial (carcinoma cell nests) compartments using image analysis applications.

sec.title: RNA and whole-exome sequencing
sec.p: RNA expression profiling was performed by Q Squared Solutions using Illumina TruSeq RNA Access chemistry on the Illumina sequencing platform with a 50 bp paired-end strategy and a target of 40 million average reads across all samples. Genomic DNA was analyzed using the Agilent SureSelect 60 Mb Kit; Exome Seq SureSelect version 6, followed by sequencing on the Illumina platform with a 63M reads 100 bp paired-end strategy.

sec.title: PTEN IHC
sec.p: PTEN protein expression was determined by IHC on 4-μm-thick FFPE sections as previously described (32–34). PTEN immunoreactivity was investigated using a rabbit monoclonal anti-PTEN antibody (#9559, clone 138G6, Cell Signaling Technology; RRID: AB_390810) and a Vectastain Elite ABC kit (Vector Laboratories). The intensity of nuclear and cytoplasmic staining was semiquantitatively assessed using the H-score formula as previously defined (33). Based on a previous PI3K inhibitor trial on solid tumors, loss of PTEN function was defined as H-score <30, with a maximum of 30% of cells at a 1+ staining intensity (26). PTEN-positive controls included normal prostate tissue and 22RV1 xenograft tissue, and PTEN-loss controls included PC3 (PTEN-null prostate cancer cell line) xenografts. Endothelial cells and stroma were used as internal positive controls for PTEN. All IHC sections were evaluated by a pathologist (B. Gurel) blinded to the patients’ clinical characteristics and outcome data.

sec.title: RNA transcriptomics analysis
sec.p: Paired-end transcriptome reads were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38) using the STAR splice-aware aligner (version 2.7.7a; RRID:SCR_004463). Raw gene expression counts were calculated with the Subread package (version 2.0.1) and used for differential expression analysis with the DESeq2 package (version 1.32.0; RRID:SCR_000154). Normalized gene expression was reported as calculated internally by DESeq2 using normalization to the geometric mean expression across replicates. Pathway enrichment scores were calculated with the GSVA package (version 1.52.3) using the zscoreParam method with default parameters. The results were obtained using the H collection of Hallmark gene sets (MSigDB version 7.0) and cell state signatures from Thommen and colleagues and Li and colleagues (Supplementary Table S5; 35, 36). Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated using the OS clinical data. P values reported were calculated using the log-rank test. Patients were stratified into low [quartile (Q) 1], medium (Q2–Q3), and high (Q4) groups by the median value of the predictor variable across the cohort.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 47 patients with advanced solid tumors or relapsed GBM were enrolled in the trial between August 2018 and September 2024 (Fig. 1). Patient demographics are described in Table 1. Patients in the solid tumor cohort A1 were heavily pretreated, having received a median of 5 (range, 1–11) prior lines of therapy for advanced disease. All patients with relapsed GBM had at least one prior line of treatment (range, 1–4). A summary of mutation distribution and immune phenotype is provided in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2. This report describes results from the proof-of-concept part A and the exploratory GBM cohort B3.

sec.title: Dose exploration
sec.p: Part A enrolled 32 patients across two planned dose levels. Accrual of patients with GBM in cohort A2 ran in parallel to the solid tumor cohort A1, with patients enrolled at the highest dose level, deemed tolerable for patients with solid tumors. As enrolment to the GBM cohort commenced prior to the publication of the 2021 World Health Organization (WHO) Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System, this cohort also included two patients with astrocytoma, isocitrate dehydrogenase mutant, WHO grade (G) 4. Although we utilized a 3 + 3 model for dose escalation in cohort A1 (only), patient recruitment continued at the RP2D to enable completion of the translational proof-of-concept studies from 12 evaluable patients. Similarly, patient recruitment continued in cohort A2 to ensure the acquisition of postdosing resection tissue from three patients (Fig. 1A).

In cohort A1, there was one DLT of G3 raised alanine aminotransferase at dose level 1 (n = 9); no DLTs were seen at dose level 2 (n = 7). There were no DLTs seen in patients with relapsed GBM across the two dose levels tested in cohort A2. The RP2D of the combination was established as oral ipatasertib 400 mg daily continuously plus intravenous atezolizumab 1,200 mg every three weeks.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: A total of 43 patients were included in the safety evaluable population. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) were reported in 43 patients, with 35 (84%) patients reporting at least one treatment-related adverse event (TRAE), defined as any TEAE deemed by the investigator to have a reasonable possibility of being caused by ipatasertib or atezolizumab (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Safety and tolerability data. Volcano plots for (A) Solid tumor cohort A1 and (B) GBM cohorts A2 and B3, listing adverse events presented as TEAEs and TRAEs by grade (NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.3). See Supplementary Table S4 for a safety data overview.

sec.p: In cohort A1 (n = 18), the most common TRAEs were G1 to G2 diarrhea (61%), rash (50%), nausea (39%), fatigue (39%), and asymptomatic transaminitis (39%), which were easily reversible. G3 TRAEs included transient and rapidly reversible rash and asymptomatic transaminitis (Fig. 2A). Hyperglycemia was mild (G1 and G2 in 6% of patients) and did not require any dose interruptions or modifications. The severity of cutaneous rashes was most pronounced in cycle 1, with subsequent habituation permitting continuation of dosing. There were no treatment-related fatalities in the study. The only G5 adverse event was a chest infection in a patient with progressive disease-related lymphangitis proven on imaging.

The safety profiles in the GBM cohorts (A2 and B3) were consistent with cohort A1, with the most common TRAEs being G1 to G2, including diarrhea (64%), rash (28%), fatigue (20%), and asymptomatic transaminitis (20%). G3 TRAEs were only seen in 8%, with rash and asymptomatic transaminitis being the most common (Fig. 2B). There were no treatment-related fatalities in the GBM cohorts.

Across all cohorts, TRAEs led to dose interruption (missed doses) in 16 patients (37.2%) and dose reduction in five patients (11.6%). The most common reasons for dose interruption and reductions were rash (32%), diarrhea (16%), transaminitis (16%), and fatigue (16%). No patient discontinued dosing due to TRAEs.

sec.title: Solid tumor cohort A1
sec.p: Two patients with metastatic treatment-refractory hormone receptor–positive breast cancer had confirmed partial responses (PR) in the cohort A1 efficacy evaluable population (n = 16). Seven patients (43.8%) had radiologic stable disease (SD), with four achieving SD >16 weeks (25%). The overall response rate was 12.5% [95% confidence interval (CI), 2.2–39.6], and the clinical benefit rate (CBR) was 37.5% (95% CI, 16.3–64.1; i.e., combined PR and SD >16 weeks). The median PFS from the start of combination therapy was 2.1 months [95% CI, 0.6 months to not reached (NR)], with a 3-month PFS rate of 33.3% (95% CI, 15.9–70) and a 6-month PFS rate of 16.7% (95% CI, 4.9–57). All five patients with breast cancer who benefited from the combination treatment (i.e., PR or SD >16 weeks) had low T-cell counts at baseline biopsies (Supplementary Table S1). Three of the patients with breast cancer benefiting from treatment (1 ER−HER2+ and 2 ER+HER2−) did not have any detectable aberration in the PI3K pathway (Supplementary Table S1).

sec.title: GBM cohorts A2 and B3
sec.p: Twenty efficacy-evaluable patients with recurrent GBM were enrolled across cohorts A2 and B3, of which 16 patients (80%) had PTEN loss by IHC (H-score <30), indicative of biallelic loss of function (Supplementary Table S2).
CBR in the overall GBM population was 30% (95% CI, 12.8–54.3), 25% (95% CI, 1.3–78.1) for PTEN intact, and 31.3% (95% CI, 12.2–58.5) for patients with PTEN loss (Fig. 3C; Supplementary Table S2).

sec.p: Additional analysis of OS from trial entry in this heavily pretreated relapsed GBM population showed a median OS of 8.81 months (95% CI, 5.52 to NR). Median OS was 8.55 months (95% CI, 4.57 to NR) for patients with PTEN loss (n = 16) and 8.81 months (95% CI, 6.84 to NR) for those with PTEN-intact tumors, respectively (Fig. 3D). The 12-month OS rate (OS12) was 33.85% (95% CI, 17.96–63.8), comparing favorably with the OS12 rate observed in contemporary recurrent GBM trials. Here, we describe three cases of patients with GBM who had prolonged responses.

A 58-year-old male (ICE101019) with recurrent GBM (PTEN loss) progressed to surgery following five cycles of ipatasertib and atezolizumab. MRI had shown an increase in contrast-enhancing disease, albeit with a significant increase in the apparent diffusion coefficient, suggestive of pseudoprogression (Fig. 3A). Histopathologic analyses of the resection sample showed maintained high levels of CD8+ lymphocyte infiltration, an increase in CD4+FOXP3− Th cells, with no residual evidence of tumor (pathologic complete response; Figs. 3A and 4G). The patient resumed treatment on trial with a PFS of 23 months.

sec.title: Treg modulation by AKT inhibition
sec.p: Ipatasertib monotherapy at the dose levels used in this study has already been shown to inhibit multiple downstream PI3K/AKT targets in paired blood and tumor samples from patients with advanced cancer, confirming target modulation of this pathway (37). We show, for the first time, that ipatasertib induces significant depletion of Tregs in both solid tumors and GBM, resulting in increased infiltration of CD8+ effector T cells in responding patients.

To quantify changes in T-cell populations in the TME, tumor biopsies were analyzed using mIF staining for T-cell markers CD4, CD8, and FOXP3. After 2 weeks of ipatasertib, at both dose levels, a reduction in CD4+ FOXP3+ Tregs in the TME was seen in cohort A1 (eight breast cancer, one cervical cancer), regardless of PIK3CA/AKT pathway mutation status (Fig. 4A and B). There were no significant changes in PD-L1 expression at these time points (Supplementary Fig. S1).

Overall, five patients with breast cancer and one patient with cervical cancer had evaluable serial biopsies at three time points: baseline, after ipatasertib (cycle 1 day 1), and following the combination of ipatasertib and atezolizumab (cycle 2 day 1). Two of the patients with PIK3CA wild-type breast cancer (1 ER+ HER2−, 1 ER+ HER2+) had a marked increase in intratumoral CD8+ T-cell infiltration by cycle 2, effectively switching from a desert phenotype to an inflamed phenotype, with clinical benefit maintained for more than four cycles (Fig. 4B and C). These findings were consistent with FACS analysis of blood samples from the entire solid tumor cohort, which showed an increase in CD8+ lymphocytes in responders after ipatasertib alone and after combination treatment (Supplementary Fig. S3).

Two patients with GBM (1 PTEN intact, 1 PTEN loss by IHC) in cohort A2 had planned re-resection of the tumor after 2 weeks of ipatasertib monotherapy for pharmacodynamic analyses (Fig. 4D). Both had reductions in CD4+FOXP3− Th cells and CD4+FOXP3+ Treg cells in the TME (Fig. 4E). At this early time point following ipatasertib monotherapy, one patient (ICE101016, PTEN intact) with a marked increase in CD8+ effector T cells achieved SD (Fig. 4E–G), whereas the other patient (ICE101038, PTEN loss), who only minimally increased CD8+ cells, had PD (Fig. 4E). The exceptional responder (ICE101019, PTEN loss), who progressed to surgery after five cycles of ipatasertib with atezolizumab, had high levels of CD8+ effector T cells at baseline, which remained elevated in the resected tumor (Fig. 4H). There was also a significant increase in CD4+FOXP3− Th cells, with no evidence of residual tumor (Figs. 3A and 4I). In all three patients, there was an increase in the Th/Treg ratio after treatment, with the greatest change seen in the exceptional responder’s surgical sample taken after the ipatasertib–atezolizumab combination. Between both patients who had samples taken after ipatasertib monotherapy, the patient who achieved SD had a greater Th/Treg shift compared with the patient who had PD (Fig. 4J). These data suggest that ipatasertib can shift CD4+ T cells toward a Th phenotype, which may correlate with response.

We investigated the archival tumor samples from all patients with GBM to identify biomarkers associated with treatment effects and clinical outcomes. We explored the impact of PTEN loss on the TME by analyzing the major immune subsets (CD8+ effector T cells, CD4+FOXP3+ Tregs, and CD4+FOXP3− Th cells) in archival samples. The abundance of these immune cells was largely similar between the PTEN intact and PTEN loss GBM tumors (Supplementary Fig. S2), consistent with our clinical observation that benefits were seen in both patient subgroups (Fig. 3C).

CD8+ effector T cells at baseline were significantly more abundant in archival tumor samples of patients with clinical benefit compared with nonresponders (Fig. 5A). Transcriptomic analysis showed that patients with clinical benefit had higher CD8A expression at baseline (Fig. 5B). Patients were stratified into CD8A mRNA low, medium, and high expression. High CD8A expression correlated with better OS (Fig. 5C).

sec.p: We then performed unsupervised clustering analysis based on activities from hallmark gene sets and correlated this with CD8A expression (Fig. 5D). All responders were in the CD8A high (4/5) and medium groups (4/10), compared with none (0/5) in the low CD8A group. Notably, 4/5 patients who had a high CD8A signature also displayed exhaustion phenotypes but then derived clinical benefit, suggesting that combination treatment was able to overcome the T-cell exhaustion state. In the CD8A medium group, 75% (3/4) of responders tended to have upregulated PI3K signaling and several inflammatory response pathways, compared with only 30% (3/10) of nonresponders. This suggests that CD8A medium tumors might rely more on PI3K activation in concert with other inflammatory pathways to achieve a response.

Additional mIF analysis of tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) was performed in three available pairs of window-of-opportunity GBM samples (Supplementary Fig. S4). In patient ICE101016, who achieved SD, post-ipatasertib samples showed a reduction in overall TAM density, including M2-like immunosuppressive subsets (Supplementary Fig. S4B and S4C). This observation, together with the previously reported reduction in Tregs in the same patient (Fig. 4E), is consistent with published reports suggesting that PI3K/AKT pathway inhibition may be associated with modulation of the immunosuppressive TME, including effects on Treg infiltration and M2 macrophage polarization. As this analysis was exploratory and not prespecified among translational endpoints, these findings require further validation.

Lastly, we compared paired serum cytokine levels taken before and after the ipatasertib run-in period. There were no significant changes in cohort A1, with no differences when comparing between response groups or PIK3CA/AKT mutation status. In the GBM cohort A2, there was suppression of IL6 in the PTEN intact group compared with PTEN loss although this difference was not observed between responders and nonresponder groups (Supplementary Fig. S5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: There remains an unmet need for effective strategies to overcome resistance to immunotherapy. Numerous studies have demonstrated that activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway in tumors promotes an immunosuppressive TME through multiple mechanisms and resistance to ICI (37). Inhibiting this pathway in combination with immunotherapy may be a strategy to improve outcomes. We present, for the first time in patients, the immunomodulatory effects of PI3K/AKT signaling pathway blockade on the TME and the preliminary efficacy of the combination of AKT inhibitor and ICI in relapsed GBM. Our clinical trial results and translational data provide further insights into targeting the PI3K/AKT pathway with brain-penetrant potent inhibitors as a promising strategy to overcome resistance to immunotherapy in GBM.

To date, most clinical studies utilizing inhibitors of the PI3K/AKT blockade have been strategically focused on combinations with endocrine therapies or chemotherapy in patient populations selected for aberrations in this pathway (e.g., PI3K mutations in breast cancer or PTEN loss in prostate cancer). A phase I combination study of the PI3Kβ-specific inhibitor GSK2636771 with pembrolizumab (NCT01458067) in patients with PTEN loss advanced cancer has recently closed. This study reported significant toxicity, with the combination RP2D using a considerably lower dose than the monotherapy dose (38). Our study shows that overall, the combination of the ATP-competitive allosteric inhibitor of AKT, ipatasertib, with atezolizumab was well tolerated, with a safety profile that was monitorable, manageable, and reversible at the RP2D. We also demonstrate, across a broad range of solid tumors and GBM, that blockade of the PI3K/AKT pathway with ipatasertib at 400 mg orally daily is associated with depletion of immunosuppressive Tregs within the TME, which does not seem to be correlated with tumor somatic PIK3CA mutational or PTEN expression status. Considerable increases in CD8+ T cells were observed in the tumors of two patients with breast cancer and one patient with GBM who benefited from the combination treatment. Notably, although ipatasertib was not designed as a brain-penetrant molecule, given the significant leakiness of the blood–brain barrier in GBM, we were able to demonstrate pharmacodynamic modulation of the immune microenvironment mirroring that seen in the patients with solid tumors, alongside preliminary clinical benefit.

Luminal (ER+) breast cancers are known to be immunologically “cold” tumors and poorly respond to single-agent ICIs. In our study, clinical benefit was observed in 50% (3/6) of patients with luminal breast cancer despite all patients having PD-L1-negative and immune desert/excluded tumors. Notably, we observed immune alterations, including Treg depletion during ipatasertib monotherapy, followed by a CD8+ T-cell increase upon the addition of atezolizumab. Together, these findings are consistent with a model in which AKT inhibition contributes to immune remodeling in otherwise immunologically cold luminal breast cancers, potentially increasing susceptibility to ICI-based therapy.

Although direct pharmacodynamic confirmation of AKT pathway inhibition in tumor biopsies was not feasible due to limited tissue availability and prioritization of immune profiling, the association between AKT inhibition and the observed immune effects is supported by multiple lines of evidence. These include the well-established on-target activity of the compound at the administered dose (37), extensive preclinical and clinical data demonstrating AKT-dependent regulation of Treg survival and function (7–11), and prior reports showing inhibition of Tregs following AKT pathway targeting (22). Finally, despite the immune changes noted after the ipatasertib run-in period, we acknowledge that definitive attribution of immune remodeling as a result of AKT inhibition alone, immune checkpoint blockade, or interactions between the two agents will require larger trials incorporating an atezolizumab-alone comparator arm. Although ICI trials have been disappointing for the treatment of GBM, it is noteworthy that a subset of our patients did respond well. There were some patients with prolonged clinical benefit and disease control, including patients with multiple relapsed GBM, a disease that is known to be resistant to immunotherapy. Analyses are only descriptive, with relatively low event numbers. Further expansion of the combination in relapsed GBM could not be pursued due to the pharmaceutical company’s strategic decision to cease development of ipatasertib in new disease areas. Future work will now focus on reverse translation into clinically relevant syngeneic models of GBM to further evaluate the potential benefit of targeting the PI3K/AKT pathway with more potent brain-penetrant inhibitors for combination strategies with immunotherapy.
